name: The Memorial Lindens of Hronsek Church

location.address: Churchyard of the Wooden Articular Church, Hronsek

access: Free to view from the churchyard of the UNESCO-listed wooden articular church, a public village church precinct. Entering the church building itself outside the main season (Sept-Jun) needs a phone booking; the courtyard and trees are not gated behind that.
transport: Hronsek village, roughly 18km / 20 minutes drive from Zvolen, no rail station in the village; regional bus from Zvolen or Banska Bystrica to Hronsek, short walk to the church.
story:
Three sources describe these lindens and no two agree on how many there are. Hronsek's own village site counts four, of which two are as old as the church. Slovak Wikipedia counts three. The national register of protected trees lists six under a single designation, the lindens by the Hronsek church. What all three agree on is the year they went in: the trees were planted when the wooden articular church was consecrated in 1726, which puts the oldest of them at roughly three centuries.

The church is what brings people to this village, and the lindens are the reason to stay another ten minutes. It was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list on 7 July 2008, one of the wooden churches of the Slovak part of the Carpathians, and these trees have stood over its shingled roof and its separate bell tower for the whole of that building's life. Every repair, every re-shingling, every winter the timber has had to survive has happened under their crowns.

Nobody has published a girth or a height for any of them, so how thick the oldest one has grown is still an open question. If you go with a tape measure, tell us.

The courtyard is a village church precinct and stands open. Getting inside the church outside the summer season needs a phone call first. The trees do not.

best_time.label: late June into July, when the limes flower and the churchyard fills with bees

name: Lipský's Lindens

location.address: Memorial park by the Ján Lipský monument, Sedličná, Trenčianske Stankovce

access: Free, in a public village memorial park with the Ján Lipský monument and bust; open ground, no ticket or booking needed.
transport: Trenčianske Stankovce village (Sedličná part), on the Trenčín-Nemšová regional bus route; nearest train station is Trenčín, then local bus or a short taxi ride.
story:
Two sources have dated the larger of these two lindens and their answers are 250 years apart. Slovak Wikipedia gives about 250 years, a girth of 630 centimetres and a height of 26 metres. The village's own official page calls the same tree roughly five hundred years old and measures it at 620 centimetres. The tape agrees to within ten centimetres. The calendar does not agree at all, and nobody has settled it. The second linden is the simpler case: around 200 years, 380 centimetres round, 24 metres tall.

They stand in the memorial park at Sedličná, above the Maxon family tomb, and they carry the name of Ján Lipský, born in this village in 1766 and buried in it in 1826. He was a cartographer and a military officer, and his monument and bust stand in the same small park.

In 2004 the pair placed third in Strom roka, Slovakia's national tree of the year vote. That is a serious result for two trees in a village most people drive past on the way to Trenčín.

Both have been protected since 21 August 1984, in the care of the Biele Karpaty landscape administration. The park is open ground, free, and there is nothing to book.

name: The Linden of Lipany

location.address: Námestie sv. Martina (St Martin's Square), by the Church of St Martin, Lipany

access: Free, standing in the pedestrianised town square in front of the Church of St Martin, open at all times.
transport: Lipany town centre; the tree stands a short walk from Lipany railway station on the Kosice-Presov-Plavec line.
story:
Lipany is named after lindens, and by local tradition this is the last one left. The town turns up in fourteenth-century records as Septemthillis, the seven lindens, and the story told here is that six are gone and this one is still standing in the square. The same tradition holds that a contract signed beneath it in front of two witnesses once carried the force of a notarial deed. Neither claim arrives with documents attached. Both are worth knowing before you stand under it.

What has actually been measured: over 320 years old, 536 centimetres round, 23 metres tall, growing in the pedestrianised square in front of the early Gothic Church of St Martin.

In 2011 it won Strom roka, Slovakia's national tree of the year vote, and the town collected a prize of 333 euro for it. The same year it went on to the European Tree of the Year contest and came fourth, ahead of a good many trees from countries with far louder publicity.

Most trees this old survived by standing where nobody needed the ground. This one has spent three centuries in the middle of a working town square, which is the harder trick. It is a short walk from Lipany station on the line from Košice through Prešov to Plaveč.

best_time.label: late June and early July, when the linden flowers and the whole square smells of it

name: The Oak of Drnava

location.address: Poklady Drnavy educational trail, stop 2, northeastern Drnava, near the former Drnava ironworks site

access: Free, standing beside the village's own "Poklady Drnavy" (Treasures of Drnava) educational trail, open ground within the built-up village.
transport: Drnava village, Roznava District; nearest railway station is Roznava, then a regional bus to Drnava.
story:
In 2020 this oak took 5,246 of the 24,839 votes cast in Strom roka and was named Slovakia's tree of the year, then went on to represent the country in the European Tree of the Year contest. Not bad for a tree standing at stop two of a village nature trail.

It is reckoned at about 700 years old and it appears in Drnava's village chronicle from 1670, which means it was already old when anyone here first thought to write it down. It is not tall: 14 metres, modest for an oak of this age, with a trunk 528 centimetres round and a crown spreading 21 metres. Ancient oaks stop reaching up and start reaching sideways, and this one has been doing that for centuries.

The ground around it has a stranger history than the tree does. Drnava was nicknamed Kis Pest, Little Pest, after the Andrássy ironworks that ran here in the nineteenth century and cast structural parts for the Chain Bridge in Budapest in the 1840s. The oak had already been in the village chronicle for 170 years by then, and it stands near that former works today.

Open ground inside the village, free, nothing to book. It sits on the Poklady Drnavy trail, the Treasures of Drnava. The nearest station is Rožňava, then a regional bus.

name: The Oak of Dubinné

location.address: Dubinné village, beside the roadside chapel

access: Free, standing on open ground in the village next to a roadside chapel, no ticket or booking needed.
transport: Dubinné village, about 15km southeast of Bardejov; reached by regional bus from Bardejov, no rail station in the village.
story:
Nobody can date this oak, because the wood that held the answer has rotted away. The village says so itself: the tree is hollow and its oldest part is irretrievably gone. What is left is a trunk 733 centimetres round at chest height, swelling to roughly twelve metres of buttressed mass at ground level, 25 metres of height, and a working figure of at least 800 years. It is widely taken to be the oldest oak in Slovakia, and in 2010 it won Strom roka, the national tree of the year vote.

Its list of near misses is long. Villagers are said to have paid a ransom to save it from felling during the Hussite wars in the middle of the fifteenth century. Soldiers used it as a reference point in both world wars. It came through the fire that burnt the village in 1913 and another in 1985 started by a smoke bomb. Lightning struck it in 1995. It is still standing.

The chapel beside it was built after an eighteenth-century report of a Marian apparition in its crown, which says more about what this tree has meant here than any contest result does.

Open ground next to the road, free, no gate. Dubinné sits about fifteen kilometres southeast of Bardejov and is reached by regional bus.

best_time.label: January and February, when the leaves are off and the hollow trunk and its flared base show in full

name: The Service Tree of Uzovská Panica
access: Free, standing in open farmland/village ground (a boundary tree historically marking property lines), no ticket or booking needed.
transport: Uzovská Panica village, Rimavská Sobota District; nearest railway/bus hub is Rimavská Sobota, then a regional bus.
story:
This tree was planted to mark where one person's land stopped and the next person's began. Service trees did that job across this part of Europe: long-lived, easy to recognise from a distance, and a signal to anyone reading the ground that the soil here was good enough for fruit. Two and a half centuries on, the boundary is a footnote and the tree is the landmark.

It is about 250 years old, which puts its planting in the reign of Maria Theresa, and it measures 295 centimetres round and 14 metres tall. It still fruits, and generously: large pear-shaped fruit, pinkish-yellow, ripening in the middle of October.

In 2019 it won Strom roka, Slovakia's national tree of the year vote, and went on to represent the country in the European Tree of the Year contest. By how much it won depends on who you ask. Ekopolis, which runs the contest, records 6,710 votes; the regional news site Rimava reported over 10,000. Neither figure has been reconciled with the other.

One naming note worth carrying with you: Sorbus domestica is the service tree, a different species from the wild service tree it gets muddled with.

It stands on open ground in the Lapoňa area of the village, free, no gate. Nearest hub is Rimavská Sobota, then a regional bus.

best_time.label: mid-October, when the pear-shaped fruit ripens pinkish-yellow

name: The Plane Tree of Budatín Park

location.address: Budatínsky park, southwestern corner of Budatín Castle wall

access: Free, standing in Budatín Park (Budatínsky park) beside Budatín Castle, an open public park at the confluence of the Kysuca and Váh rivers.
transport: Žilina; Budatín Park is a short walk or local bus ride from Žilina railway station.
story:
Two planes stand at the southwestern corner of Budatín Castle's wall with their roots grown into each other. One of them represented Slovakia at a European contest. The other has been struck by lightning and is being worked on from the inside by a wood-rotting fungus.

The healthy one is the larger of the pair and the biggest of several planes in the park: 603 centimetres round, 27 metres tall, about 270 years old. It won Strom roka, the national tree of the year vote, in 2016, and came ninth of sixteen at the European Tree of the Year contest the following year.

Its planting comes with a date and two names attached, which is unusual for a tree this old. In 1745 Count Ján Sunyog brought a gardener called František Roder over from Silesia to lay out the grounds around the castle, and this plane went in as part of that work. It has stood against the same wall ever since, through every change of owner and every change of use the castle has been put to.

The park lies where the Kysuca runs into the Váh, on the northern edge of Žilina. It is open public ground, free, and a short walk or local bus ride from the railway station.

name: The Lindens of Kysucká Street
verified_sources: https://www.npmalafatra.sk (2022-05 arborist care article on these two lindens)
access: Free, standing beside Kysucká cesta, a public street in Žilina, no ticket or booking needed.
transport: Žilina; a short walk or local bus ride from Žilina railway station, about 400m from the Budatín Park plane tree.
story:
Nobody has recorded how old these two lindens are. No register carries an age for them, no source carries a girth, and the only figure anybody has published is the count: two. They are protected regardless, listed in the national register of protected trees as the lindens of Žilina, and they are in the care of the Malá Fatra National Park administration, whose day job is a mountain range outside the city.

That care is real rather than nominal. In spring 2022 an arborist crew pruned both trees for safety and health and fitted new dynamic support cables to the larger of the pair, the kind of rigging that lets a heavy limb keep moving in the wind while catching it if it ever lets go. One of the two is in visibly better condition than the other, which is roughly what you would expect of street trees on a road like Kysucká cesta, taking traffic, salt and road works for however many decades they have stood there.

They are about 400 metres from the plane tree in Budatín Park, close enough that the two make one short walk rather than two separate trips.

The open question stays open. If you know when these limes went in, or you have put a tape around one of them, tell us and we will put the number on this page.

name: The Maple of Sokolovská Street
species: Maple (Acer sp.); the register calls it javor cukrovy (usually Acer saccharum, Sugar Maple) but sk.wikipedia's own protected-tree list gives the binomial as Acer saccharinum (Silver Maple) for this same row, a genuine source conflict left for the reader/a botanist to settle in person
access: Free, standing beside Sokolovská ulica, a public street in Žilina, no ticket or booking needed.
transport: Žilina; a short walk or local bus ride from Žilina railway station, about 1.5km from the Budatín Park plane tree.
story:
Two sources name this tree and they differ by two letters. The national register calls it javor cukrový, sugar maple, which is Acer saccharum. Slovak Wikipedia's own list of protected trees gives the binomial for that same row as Acer saccharinum, the silver maple. Both are North American, both were planted along European streets in the nineteenth century, and the difference is readable from the pavement: a silver maple's leaves are deeply cut and near-white underneath, so they flash pale when the wind turns them. Nobody has settled which of the two grows on Sokolovská. If you know your maples and you walk past, look up and tell us.

What the two sources agree on is that it is worth keeping. The register lists it as the only specimen of its species of any real age in the district, which is why it was designated in the first place. That is a modest claim and an honest one: this is not an ancient tree, it is an unusual one that has been allowed to get old on a city street.

No age has been recorded and no girth measured, so how long it has stood here is open too.

It is about 1.5 kilometres from the plane in Budatín Park and 1.2 kilometres from the protected limes on Kysucká cesta. Three protected trees, one afternoon.

name: The Great Chestnut of Časta

location.address: In the vineyards above Časta village

verified_sources: https://ekopolis.sk (Strom roka coverage of this tree, cited in the earlier research note carried over below)
access: Free, standing in open vineyard ground above the village, reachable on foot from Časta; not fenced or gated.
transport: Časta village, Pezinok District, about 34km from Bratislava; regional bus from Pezinok or Modra, then a short walk uphill into the vineyards.
story:
Slovakia's largest sweet chestnut does not grow in a park or an arboretum. It stands out in the vineyards on the slope above Časta, roughly 500 years old, with a trunk that sources put at between 830 and 866 centimetres and a height somewhere between 23 and 25 metres. Take the conservative end of both figures and it is still more than eight metres round.

Eight metres of chestnut is a particular sight. The species twists its bark into spiralling ridges as it ages, so an old trunk looks wrung out rather than smooth, and the biggest one in the country is where that is easiest to see. In October the spiny burrs come down and the ground underneath takes some walking across.

It has been protected since the end of the 1990s, although the sources cannot agree whether the designation came in December 1997 or in 1998. A year either way makes little difference to a tree that was already four centuries old when the paperwork began.

Getting there involves a walk, which is part of the point. Časta lies about 34 kilometres from Bratislava, reached by regional bus from Pezinok or Modra, and the tree is uphill from the village in open vineyard ground. Nothing is fenced, nothing is ticketed, and the view back down the slope comes free with it.

best_time.label: October, when the burrs split and the chestnuts drop into the vineyard grass
